subject: Edgecraft discovery: competitive latency readout + next bench steps
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Evelyn Park <evelyn.park@edgecraft.ai>, Tom Liu <tom.liu@edgecraft.ai>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>, Sofia Ivanova <sofia@redwood.com>
Date: 2029-08-15T13:08:00-07:00
Subject: Edgecraft discovery: competitive latency readout + next bench steps

Thanks again for the call this morning — great context on the inference patterns you’re seeing for multimodal search and routing. Quick recap and a concrete bench proposal so we can get apples-to-apples numbers vs the hyperscaler tests you already ran.

Recap (high level):
- Primary SLOs: p95 latency under 180ms for short-text queries (<=128 tokens), p99 under 350ms; sustained tokens/sec target ~8k for mixed user traffic.
- Current hyperscaler baseline you provided: p95 ~210–260ms, p99 ~420–520ms depending on the model family.
- Key workload characteristics: many short prefix-heavy prompts, sporadic long-form synth requests, and a heavy tail of concurrent sessions at peak.

Where Redwood stands (differentiators relevant to these tests):
- Adaptive KV prefix caching to avoid re-computation on short-prefix queries; we expect ~25–40% p95 improvement on prefix-heavy traffic vs unoptimized endpoints.
- Smart batching with latency-aware boundaries (we enforce a 30ms batching window for throughput without violating p95 SLOs).
- Quantization profiles tuned per-model to reduce GPU memory pressure and increase effective tokens/sec without measurable quality loss on your eval set.
- Routing fallbacks: automatically route to a lower-cost compatible variant if capacity spikes — keeps errors and tail latencies down.

Proposed bench plan (attached as edgecraft_latency_testplan.xlsx, summary below):
1) Replicate your hyperscaler run (same model family, seq length distribution, and token mix).
2) Run Redwood baseline (no KV cache, default batching) to validate parity.
3) Run Redwood tuned: KV cache + latency-aware batching + quantized model variant.
4) A/B comparison: measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and CPU/GPU utilization across runs; include a 60-minute steady-state window and two 10-minute burst windows.

Concrete asks from Edgecraft to proceed:
- Can you share the exact replay trace (or a 30–60 minute sample trace) you used with the hyperscaler? ideal: req timestamp, prompt length, model name, and concurrency envelope.
- Confirmation of the model family and precision (e.g., Falcon-40B-Base / FP16) used in your earlier tests.

Next steps / schedule:
- If you can drop the trace and confirm model details by EOD Friday (8/16), our infra team will provision a dedicated experiment pool and share preliminary numbers by Tuesday (8/20).
- Ben, can you please confirm resource availability and whether we should allocate a Dedicated pool for the first run?

Thanks — tagging Ben and Sofia for lab ops and instrumentation notes.

—
Marissa Cole
Senior Account Exec, Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.com | +1 415-555-0128
Redwood Inference

Attachments: edgecraft_latency_testplan.xlsx (spreadsheet: test matrix, traffic profiles); redwood_offer_v1.pdf (high-level license/price options)

From: Evelyn Park <evelyn.park@edgecraft.ai>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Tom Liu <tom.liu@edgecraft.ai>
Date: 2029-08-15T16:22:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Edgecraft discovery: competitive latency readout + next bench steps

Marissa — thanks for the write-up and clear plan. A few clarifications from our side: 

1) Replay trace: attaching a 45-minute sample (anonymized) in the Drive link below. The trace includes timestamps, token counts, and request IDs. We scrubbed PII.
2) Hyperscaler config: we used Falcon-40B in FP16, Standard instance type (mGPUs), autoscaling enabled.
3) Concurrency envelope: typical bursts up to 380 concurrent sessions; sustained background at ~180.

We are most interested in: p99 tail behavior during bursts and whether Redwood’s KV caching will impact throughput on mixed-length traffic. Also want to verify req->response error rate under fallback routing.

We can confirm the trace and model details by EOD today. For the first run we prefer you use a Dedicated pool so results are not noisy from multi-tenant burst activity.

Two scheduling notes:
- Can you share an expected time budget (hours) and a rough cost estimate for the three-run matrix?
- If results look promising we’ll want to schedule a follow-up technical review with our infra lead (Tom) and the platform SRE.

—
Evelyn Park
Head of AI Engineering, Edgecraft
evelyn.park@edgecraft.ai

Related link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/Edgecraft-SampleTrace

Looping in operational details — we can carve out a dedicated GPU pool for the first experiment. Notes for the run: 
- Provision 4x A100-80GB equiv (or an N variant that matches Falcon-40B throughput) for initial parity runs. If the team prefers a cheaper quantized variant we can scale back to 2x and run the quantized profile there.
- Instrumentation: please ensure the replay contains request IDs so we can align traces. We’ll push per-request latency and GPU kernel times to the shared Drive CSV.
- Cost estimate (very rough): parity run ~ $1,100 for 1-hour steady-state + bursts; tuned run (quantized + cache) ~ $750; full three-run matrix including provisioning/buffer ~ $3,200. Final numbers depend on run length and provisioning window.

Marissa — I’ll draft a short-runbook and attach the instrumentation checklist. Sofia — can you validate the telemetry hooks (trace id, model variant tag, cache hit metric) before we kick off?

—

- Error/fallback behavior: we’ll include a fault-injection pass (short 5-minute period) to validate routing fallback and error-rate behavior — results will include failover counts and tail latency breakdowns.

Next milestones:
